# SVAEval: An Evaluation Framework for LLM-based SVA Property Generators

Yu-An Shih, SooHyuk Cho, Aarti Gupta and Sharad Malik Princeton University, Princeton, USA {yashih, soohyuk.cho}@princeton.edu, aartig@cs.princeton.edu, sharad@princeton.edu Artifact Available

Abstract—Assertion-based verification (ABV) uses SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) to formally specify design behavior, but constructing high-quality SVA properties remains a labor-intensive and error-prone process. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled automated SVA generation from design specification documents; however, there are limitations in how the quality of the generated SVA properties, and thus the SVA generator, is evaluated. Existing automatic evaluation methods rely on formal tools – such as model checking and coverage analysis – to measure the correctness and completeness of the generated properties against a golden RTL implementation. However, it is difficult to obtain bug-free RTL designs, and even if they are available, the computed metrics do not accurately reflect the quality of generated properties against design specifications. We propose SVAEVAL, an automatic approach to evaluate SVA property generators, by directly evaluating the generated property sets without the need of golden RTL implementations. SVAEVAL considers two different scenarios: (1) If a humanexpert-generated golden SVA property set is available (e.g., in a benchmark set), a formal framework is used to accurately evaluate the quality of the generated property set against the golden set. (2) Without a golden SVA property set, a hybrid formal and LLM-based framework is used to compare the quality of two generated property sets from different SVA generators. Experimental results demonstrate that SVAEVAL provides significantly more reliable evaluation than prior approaches, and offer new insights into the capabilities and limitations of various LLM-based SVA property generators. Index Terms—Assertion-based verification (ABV), SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), Large Language Models (LLMs), property generation, evaluation methodologies

I. INTRODUCTION

Assertion-based verification (ABV) [1] is a core methodology in modern hardware design, enabling designers to formally specify hardware properties using temporal logic. These properties, usually written in SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) [2], specify both legal input from the environment (assumptions) and expected design behavior (assertions). These SVA properties are concurrent assertions, which are temporal properties that hold for the entire design, in contrast to immediate assertions, which hold at some point in the code. The registertransfer level (RTL) design is then verified with simulation or formal verification to ensure that all assertions pass under the assumptions.

However, developing high-quality SVA properties for industrial designs is a labor-intensive process. Verification engineers read design specification documents, identify relevant information for verification, and translate those natural language descriptions into SVA properties. This process is timeconsuming and error-prone, often requiring multiple iterations before a correct and complete property set is constructed [3]. Recent research has explored the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to assist human engineers in generating SVA properties from natural language specifications, including sentence/paragraph-level NL-to-SVA translation [4]–[9] and end-to-end SVA generation frameworks [10]–[17]. While these approaches show promise in reducing manual effort, there is a lack of reliable evaluation methods to determine how well the generated properties reflect the intended design behavior. An SVA property set should be evaluated in various aspects: (1) correctness, ensuring that the properties are consistent with the specification; and (2) completeness: ensuring that all required design constraints in the specification are captured. An additional feature is (3) usefulness, ensuring that each property contributes to meaningful design behavior, instead of being a tautology or a redundant property. In a typical functional verification flow, both correctness and completeness gradually improve throughout the verification process. For example, when the design contradicts an assertion, verification engineers analyze the root cause and determine whether to report a hardware bug or modify the assertion. For completeness, coverage analysis tools [18] are used to identify portions in the design that are not covered by any assertions, providing hints towards adding more design constraints. Usefulness is usually implicitly guaranteed by the expertise of human engineers. Recent works on LLM-based SVA generation often rely on automatic tools to evaluate the quality of generated properties with golden, i.e., bug-free, RTL implementations [11], [13]– [16] of the design specification. For example, to measure correctness, model checkers [19] are used to formally verify the generated assertions, marking the passed assertions as correct. Coverage analysis tools are then used to compute the coverage of these passed assertions on the RTL implementation, as a measurement of completeness. A challenge for this evaluation paradigm is the difficulty in obtaining a bug-free RTL design. In academia, where

II. RTL-IMPLEMENTATION-BASED EVALUATION

Recent research on LLM-based SVA generation relies on automatic tools to evaluate the generated properties against golden, i.e., bug-free, RTL implementations [11], [13]–[16]. However, the correctness and completeness of an SVA property set should be assessed with reference to the specification rather than to a valid implementation. This mismatch, without proper manual inspection, introduces inaccuracy regarding the quality of the generated properties. Without loss of generality, we focus on two most widely used evaluation methods in recent literature – model checking to evaluate correctness, and coverage analysis to evaluate completeness. We discuss sources of their inaccuracies and provide real-world examples. Practical experimental results demonstrating these inaccuracies are shown in Section IV-C.

We identify multiple sources of inaccuracies for this evaluation strategy, as listed below. 1) Tautologies and redundant properties: LLMs generate tautologies and redundant properties (Figs. 1 and 2). These properties pass assertion checks, increasing correctness number/rate without adding value to the entire property set. 2) Under-/Over-constrained assumption sets: Assumptions cannot be verified using an RTL design, since they are environment constraints that specify legal inputs instead of expected design behaviors. However, while coverage analysis is helpful in assisting thorough design verification, it does not directly measure how well the SVA properties capture the requirements in the specification documents. Various coverage analysis techniques exist, each providing different trade-offs between accuracy and computational cost. Without loss of generality, we discuss two techniques supported by JasperGold [21], a widely used industrial formal verification platform. 1) Cone-of-influence (COI) Analysis: This method performs structural analysis to identify all design signals and logic elements within the fan-in cone of the assertions. Though computationally inexpensive, this metric is very inaccurate. For example, tautologies contribute to COI coverage. An LLM which generates tautologies that include all design signals can achieve 100% COI coverage despite being totally useless. 2) Proof Core Analysis: This method leverages model checking to identify the subset of design logic that is required to prove an assertion. The resulting proof core represents the minimal or near-minimal portion of the design necessary to establish correctness, making it more accurate than COI analysis. However, the dependence on model checking also leads to its own sources of inaccuracies: (1) the assumptions do not contribute to coverage since their proof core cannot be computed; (2) the RTL design may only implement a subset of specified design behaviors. III. SVAEVAL EVALUATION METHODOLOGIES

This section describes the methods and algorithms of SVAEVAL. We consider two scenarios: If a golden SVA property set is provided (scenario 1), the SVAEVAL-FORMAL framework is used to formally evaluate any test property sets; Without golden SVA property sets (scenario 2), the SVAEVAL-HYBRID framework combines formal and LLMbased techniques to compare different test property sets.

A. Scenario 1: With Golden SVA Property Sets

A golden SVA property set, denoted G = {g1, g2, ..., gm}, is a formal specification that defines all valid execution traces of the design. That is,

τ ∈T is valid ⇔∀g ∈G, τ |= g

where T denotes the set of all possible traces over the set of signals from the specification. Given the golden property set, we can formally evaluate the correctness, completeness, and usefulness of any LLMgenerated property set (T = {t1, t2, ..., tn}).

• Correctness: A property t ∈T is incorrect, or overconstrained, if there exists a valid execution trace of the design that violates the property. That is,

t is incorrect in T ⇔∃τ ∈T , τ |= G ∧τ ̸|= t,

where τ |= G is a short-hand for ∀g ∈G, τ |= g.

• Completeness: T is complete if and only if it eliminates all invalid design behaviors. This means that every valid trace of T should also be a valid trace of G. Therefore, if a valid trace of T violates any property g ∈G, then T is incomplete, and g is a missing property in T:

g is missing in T ⇔∃τ ∈T , τ |= T ∧τ ̸|= g.

• Usefulness: We say a property t is useless, or redundant, if it does not add new constraints to the set. That is, any trace that satisfies T \ {t} also satisfies t:

t is redundant in T ⇔∀τ ∈T , τ |= T \ {t} ⇒τ |= t.

A special category of useless properties is tautology, where the property is satisfied by any possible trace:

t is a tautology ⇔∀τ ∈T , τ |= t.

We implement the above checks with a model checker, where T is represented as a free unconstrained model over symbolic inputs, i.e., it can produce all possible sequences of signal values in the specification. We use JasperGold (version 2021.03) [21] as the model checker in our experiments. We develop iterative algorithms that use these checks to identify incorrect, missing, tautological, and redundant properties from the LLM-generated property sets. For example,

To obtain accurate results, the correctness check should precede completeness and redundancy checks. Otherwise, incorrect properties in T might cause the following checks to (1) fail to detect missing properties and (2) mark irredundant properties as redundant. For example, consider the extreme case where an LLM generated the property assert 1’b0 in T. Since no execution trace satisfies this property, it can be seen from the above equations that (1) none of the properties in G would be marked as missing, and (2) all other properties in T would be marked as redundant. Therefore, all incorrect (over-constrained) properties should be removed before the completeness and redundancy checks. The tautology check is independent of the others. We run it first simply because it is fast and reduces the input size for other algorithms. Ideally, a golden property set should correctly and completely reflect the intent of its natural language specification and should contain no useless properties. For complex design protocols, however, it is difficult to ensure that a property set is complete with respect to the entire specification. Fortunately, a human-generated property set doesn’t have to be complete for the evaluation to be accurate. Instead, the correctness check will remain accurate as long as the humangenerated set, denoted G′, satisfies the following conditions: (1) Every property in G′ is correct. This ensures that any incorrect property in T is detected. (2) G′ is more complete than any test property set T it compares to, i.e., any property t ∈T, if correct, should also be covered by G′. This will

B. Scenario 2: Without Golden SVA Property Sets

Without a golden SVA property set, the only ground truth for evaluating the correctness and completeness of a test property set is the informal specification document. While it is common to use LLM-as-a-judge [22] in such a setting, relying solely on LLMs can lead to unreliable assessments. In particular, when the LLMs used by the SVA generator and the judge possess similar reasoning limitations, the judge may fail to identify incorrect or incomplete properties from the generated SVA property sets, thereby reducing the reliability of the evaluation process. We propose SVAEVAL-HYBRID, a hybrid formal and LLMbased approach that compares the relative correctness and completeness of two test property sets, allowing us to compare different SVA generators. The comparison algorithm is shown in Fig. 6. 1) Identifying Unique Properties: A property t in Test Set 1 (T1) is unique with respect to Test Set 2 (T2) if it creates additional constraints when added to T2. That is, there exists a valid execution trace of T2 that violates t:

is unique(t, T2) ⇔∃τ ∈T , τ |= T2 ∧τ ̸|= t.

This check is used to identify unique properties from both property sets. Note that these unique properties are where the two SVA generators disagree with each other, and it is not clear if each of them is correct or incorrect. 2) CEX-supported LLM-based Correctness Check: When the model checker identifies a unique property t, it also provides the corresponding counterexample (CEX) trace τ. This CEX is used by an Evaluation LLM (effectively serving as an LLM-judge) in conjunction with the design documents to help determine the correctness of the property. If the CEX is a valid execution trace of the design, then the unique property, which it violates, is deemed to be incorrect. If the CEX is invalid, then it increases the confidence that the property is correct. In the absence of a formal ground truth, at some point we will need to rely on an LLM-judge. Providing the LLMjudge with a CEX increases its overall success as compared to providing the property alone. 3) Iterative Comparison: After removing incorrect properties, the formal method may identify new unique properties.

We discuss the inaccuracies of the comparison algorithm that are intrinsic to the lack of a formal ground-truth and intrinsic to the overall dependence of LLMs for automation. First, since the shared incorrect properties cannot be detected by the formal methods, they will remain in the combined property check. However, this does not affect the accuracy in comparing the relative correctness and completeness of the two sets. In contrast, incorrect LLM decisions affect both the comparison and the combined property set. These include (1) false positives, where uniquely incorrect properties are categorized as correct and put into the combined set; and (2) false negatives, where uniquely correct properties are categorized as incorrect and discarded. The redundancy check is also affected by previous inaccuracies in the comparison algorithm. Specifically, if incorrect properties are undetected and remain in the set, they may cause other correct properties to appear redundant. IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

To demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed evaluation methodologies, we selected 4 hardware protocols [23]– [26] as our test cases, as shown in Table I. Existing opensource works have developed formal specifications for these protocols [12], [20]. Building upon these efforts, we carefully construct golden property sets that correctly and completely reflect their design specification documents. Compared with the other test cases, AXI is substantially more complex due to its multiple independent channels, support for outstanding and out-of-order transactions, burst transfers, and numerous optional features. Therefore, our manually created property set is not complete (compared to the AMBA 3 AXI Protocol Checker User Guide released by ARM [27]). We mitigate this by removing several sections in the specification document that explain certain features (cache support, protection unit support, and atomic accesses), thereby focusing on a well-defined subset of the protocol. Moreover, we ensure that our golden property set is more complete than any test set by manually inspecting the result of the correctness check, as discussed in Section III-A, to ensure the accuracy of the SVAEVAL-FORMAL framework. To compare SVAEVAL with previous RTL-implementationbased evaluation methods, we obtain 3 open-source RTL designs that implement these protocols. The WISHBONE DMA/Bridge IP Core (wb_dma), obtained from Open- Cores [28], provides DMA transfers between two WISHBONE interfaces, each containing a master and slave. The core is extended with the Q-Channel low-power interface and used as a test case in an EDA project [29]. The APB and AXI RAM modules (apb_ram, axi_ram) are obtained from the Taxi Transport Library [30]. We evaluate various SVA generation techniques, using different models, as shown in columns 1-2 of Table II:

• Zero-shot prompting: Our baseline method uses a simple prompt in a zero-shot setting to ask LLMs to generate SVA properties from design specifications. To compare LLMs with different reasoning capabilities, we select the frontier GPT-5.4 model and the deprecated GPT-4o model in our experiments.

• Multi-stage SVA generation: Numerous end-to-end frameworks decompose SVA generation into multiple tasks, each targeted by specialized LLMs [11], [13]– [17]. We select SANGAM [15], one of the state-of-the-art

among these frameworks. SANGAM consists of 3 main steps: (1) Specification Processing, which uses 3 LLMs to extract signal-wise information from the document; (2) Assertion Reasoning, using a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based algorithm to expand and fix the property sets based on feedback from both LLMs and the Cadence JasperGold Formal Verification tool [21]; and (3) Assertion Combination, a final stage that de-duplicates all generated properties with an LLM to produce the final set. Again, we run the SANGAM framework with GPT-5.4 and GPT-4o in our experiments.

• Fine-tuning LLMs for NL-to-SVA translation: Recent works have also fine-tuned LLMs to improve sentencelevel NL-to-SVA translation [9], [31]. For example, QiMeng-CodeV-SVA [9] provided an NL-SVA dataset with 83K instances, and fine-tuned open-source models into CodeV-SVA, a series of models specialized for NLto-SVA translation. They also applied CodeV-SVA to an end-to-end SVA generation framework [32], replacing the LLM used in the NL-to-SVA stage with CodeV- SVA, demonstrating an increased number of syntactically correct and FPV passed assertions. Our SANGAM+QiMeng setting uses the SANGAM framework but replaces the NL-to-SVA model with Qwen3-8B and its fine-tuned CodeV-SVA-8B, to evaluate the effectiveness of this method.

VI. LIMITATIONS

Dependence on formal semantics. Our evaluation methodology is fundamentally based on formal verification and symbolic model checking. As a result, our framework also inherits the limitations of formal verification tools. For example, hardware description languages such as SystemVerilog are naturally expressed using four-state logic (0/1/X/Z). In simulation-based verification, unknown (X) and high-impedance (Z) values are explicitly represented and often play an important role in RTL debugging. In contrast, formal verification tools generally interpret X and Z as unconstrained symbolic choices in two-state (0/1) logic. Consequently, properties that explicitly depend on four-state logic may not be meaningfully evaluated in our framework. For example, the $isunknown(<signal>) construct is typically reduced to false during formal analysis. We exclude any properties that contain simulation-oriented semantics from our experiments. Dependence on Specification Documents. Our methodology assumes that all the intended design behaviors are described in available specification documents. However, in industrial practice, specifications are often incomplete or even absent, especially for emerging designs. Even for designs implementing standardized protocols, specification documents typically describe only architectural behavior. RTL designs frequently contain micro-architectural optimizations for performance and power concerns, which will not be captured by the architecture-level specifications. As a consequence, verification engineers sometimes work with the RTL design itself, with little or no reference from specification documents, to develop SVA properties. Recent research has also explored this direction, developing LLM-based techniques to generate SVA properties from both specifications and RTL designs [31]–[41], or even from RTL designs alone [42]–[44]. Similarly, current works rely on the inaccurate implementation-based methods to evaluate the generated SVA properties. Developing reliable evaluation methodologies for RTL-centric SVA generation requires entirely different mindsets, and remains an important direction for future research.

VII. RELATED WORK

NL2SVA evaluation methods. Recent works have proposed benchmarks that translate high-level NL description to SVA properties (NL2SVA). FVEval [45] constructed both realworld and synthetic benchmarks to evaluate the ability of various LLMs in generating syntactically and functionally correct SVA properties. Hybrid-NL2SVA [31] and QiMeng-CodeV- SVA [9] focused on developing high-quality benchmarks to

fine-tune open-source models. Hybrid-NL2SVA collected 4K SVAs from hardware verification textbooks; QiMeng-CodeV- SVA used LLMs to generate NL-SVA pairs from RTL code and performs distillation to obtain 83K instances. To evaluate functional correctness, these works utilize formal verification tools to check the exact logical equivalence between a pair of model-generated and ground-truth properties. In contrast, our work focuses on evaluating end-to-end SVA generation from design specification documents. SVAEVAL compares the correctness, completeness, and usefulness of entire SVA property sets. Assessing importance of individual properties. Beyond correctness, recent work has also explored estimating the relative importance of individual properties. Spec2Assertion [14] proposes an importance score computed using signal dependency graphs extracted from RTL designs, where properties spanning longer dependency paths are assigned higher scores. This approach is complementary to ours and can be applied to evaluate different aspects of a generated SVA property set.

VIII. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS

We present SVAEVAL, an evaluation framework for LLMbased SVA generators, which operates under two scenarios: (1) With golden SVA property sets developed by human experts, SVAEVAL-FORMAL implements a formal framework to evaluate the correctness, completeness and usefulness of generated SVA property sets; (2) Without golden SVA property sets, SVAEVAL-HYBRID implements a hybrid formal and LLM-based framework to compare different generated SVA property sets. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of SVAEVAL over existing RTL-implementationbased evaluation methods. Based on the results, we analyze the effectiveness of various SVA generation techniques and discuss remaining challenges. Currently, our evaluation dataset remains relatively small due to the significant effort required for manual construction and validation. As LLM-based SVA generators continue to improve, larger and more diverse benchmarks will become increasingly important for reliable evaluation. Recent research in a software security has explored using a reliable comparison framework to help revising formal specifications [46]. For SVA generation, SVAEVAL-HYBRID provides a promising direction towards this goal, since it enables the combination of SVA property sets from multiple generators into progressively improved property sets without requiring exhaustive manual inspection. For future work, we plan to leverage this framework to construct a continuously expanding and progressively improving dataset for future research on automated SVA generation and evaluation.

# Flag: Formal and LLM-assisted SVA Generation for Formal Specifications of On-Chip Communication Protocols

**Authors:** Yu-An Shih, Annie Lin, Aarti Gupta and Sharad Malik Affiliation: Princeton University, Princeton, USA {yashih, al2413}@princeton.edu, aarti@cs.princeton.edu, sharad@princeton.edu

## Abstract

Formal specifications of on-chip communication protocols are crucial for system-on-chip (SoC) design and verification. However, manually constructing these formal specifications from informal documents remains a tedious and error-prone task. Although recent efforts have used Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) properties from design documents for Register-Transfer Level (RTL) design verification, in our experience these approaches have not shown promise in generating SVA properties for communication protocols. Since protocol specification documents are unstructured and ambiguous in nature, LLMs often fail to extract the necessary information and end up generating irrelevant or even incorrect properties.

We propose Flag, a two-stage framework to help construct formal protocol specifications from informal documents. In the first stage, a predefined template set is used to generate candidate SVA properties. To avoid missing necessary properties, we develop a grammar-based approach to generate comprehensive template sets that capture critical signal behaviors for various communication protocols. In the second stage, we utilize unambiguous timing diagrams in conjunction with textual descriptions from the specification documents to filter out incorrect properties. A formal approach is first implemented to check the candidate properties and filter out those inconsistent with the timing diagrams. An LLM is then consulted to further remove incorrect properties with respect to the textual description, obtaining the final property set. Experiments on various open-source communication protocols demonstrate the effectiveness of Flag in generating SVA properties from informal documents.

#### Index Terms:

## I Introduction

Modern system-on-chips (SoCs) rely on standardized on-chip communication protocols (e.g., AXI [1], WISHBONE [2] and PCI [3]) to regulate the interaction between various hardware intellectual properties (IPs). These protocols define the rules and mechanisms for data exchange between multiple hardware components, ensuring efficient and reliable communication between processors, memory, and peripherals.

As a consequence, formal specifications of these protocols play a crucial role in SoC design and verification [4, 5, 6, 7]. A formal specification consists of a set of temporal properties that regulate the behavior of interface signals between multiple hardware components. These properties, typically written in SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) [8], are used to debug hardware components through assertion-based verification (ABV) [9]. In addition to hardware design verification, these formal specifications are used in various electronic design automation (EDA) tasks, including hardware synthesis [10, 11].

Protocol specification documents are often written informally in natural languages to assist hardware design engineers in developing systems and modules compatible with the protocol. To construct a formal specification, verification engineers have to read the document, extract relevant information about signal interaction rules, and translate them into formal properties [4]. This process can be tedious and error-prone. Moreover, each time the protocol is updated to a new version, the specification has to be modified accordingly. Therefore, there is generally a lack of open-source formal protocol specifications despite the wide adoption of ABV.

Recent research has explored the use of machine learning (ML), including Large Language Models (LLMs), to generate SVA properties from IC design specification documents [12, 13, 14]. The primary goal of these works is to support RTL design and verification. ML models are consulted to extract information from documents and translate them into SVA properties. The results are evaluated using metrics such as number of generated assertions and cone-of-influence (COI) coverage. However, in our experience, the problem of generating formal specifications for communication protocols brings new challenges that are not solved by these approaches.

First, a formal protocol specification requires the exact information that describes how interactions between signals are regulated. As specification documents typically consist of hundreds of pages, we find that it is very difficult for ML models to understand which information to extract. If applied directly, they end up missing necessary properties while generating many irrelevant ones.

Second, statements in informal protocol specifications are meant to be read by experienced human engineers. Some of these can be ambiguous or difficult to understand for ML models. As shown in Fig. 1, it can be intuitive to translate an ambiguous natural language statement into an incorrect SVA property. In fact, ML models in previous works [15, 16] have made the exact type of mistake shown in Fig. 1, when translating natural language sentences into SVAs.

Natural Language statement DATA must remain stable when VALID is asserted and READY is LOW. Incorrect SVA property (VALID && !READY) |-> $stable(DATA) Correct SVA property (VALID && !READY) |-> ##1 $stable(DATA)

*Fig. 1: Example of an ambiguous statement. An ML model may intuitively translate “remain stable” into the $stable operator in SVA. However, the “remain stable” in this context actually means “assign the same value in the next clock cycle,” i.e., the $stable operator should be delayed by one cycle.*

To address these issues, we propose Flag (Formal and LLM-assisted Assertion Generation), a two-stage framework to assist its user in generating formal protocol specifications from informal documents (Fig. 2). In addition to LLM-based techniques, Flag combines a template-based property generation method and a formal property check algorithm to obtain accurate SVA properties.

*Fig. 2: The Flag framework.*

In the first stage, Flag generates a set of candidate properties based on a predefined template set. A grammar-based approach is developed to generate the template set, where the grammar is constructed by studying signal behaviors of various on-chip communication protocols. Compared to ML-based methods, this approach avoids missing necessary properties or generating irrelevant ones. Another advantage of the template-based approach is that it guarantees 100% syntax correctness and improves readability, while LLMs can use complex syntax for simple properties or even make syntax errors.

In the second stage, Flag utilizes timing diagrams in the specification documents to formally check the candidate properties. Unlike natural language descriptions, these timing diagrams describe signal behavior in a cycle-by-cycle manner and are thus unambiguous in nature. For example, one can easily distinguish the correct and incorrect SVA properties depicted in Fig. 1 by observing the timing diagrams in Fig. 3. By filtering out properties that are inconsistent with the timing diagrams, we reduce the chance of obtaining incorrect properties due to text ambiguity. However, note that some incorrect properties may still be consistent with the descriptive timing diagrams in the document.

Therefore, given the formally checked properties, we prompt an LLM to further filter out incorrect properties with respect to a textual description extracted from the specification document. The key concept is that LLMs are now used to compare the textual descriptions with a set of formally generated properties, instead of being asked to generate SVA properties provided only the massive and unstructured documents. With this approach, we mitigate the risks of missing necessary properties and generating incorrect or irrelevant properties from ML models.

*(b) READY before VALID.*

*Fig. 3: Example of timing diagrams extracted from the AMBA AXI Protocol Specification [1].*

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- • We propose Flag, a template-based framework that combines formal and LLM-based techniques to help generate formal protocol specifications from informal documents.

- • We develop a grammar-based approach to generate and maintain template sets for the Flag framework, and construct a grammar that can be used to generate SVAs for various on-chip communication protocols.

- • The effectiveness of Flag is evaluated on various real-world communication protocols. This includes a comparison with a state-of-the-art approach for SVA generation from design specification documents.

We publicly release our code and experiments at https://github.com/Yu-An-Shih/FLAG.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the overview of our approach. Section III and IV explain the details of our algorithms. In Section V, we evaluate each step of our algorithms, and compare our results with a state-of-the-art SVA generation framework. Section VI indicates limitations of our framework, and Section VII discusses related works. Finally, we provide concluding remarks and indicate future directions in Section VIII.

## II Overview

The overall workflow of our Flag framework is shown in Fig. 2. This section provides an overview of each step to describe how the framework assists its users in generating SVA properties from specification documents.

User Input. To begin with, the user extracts a group of timing diagrams from the specification documents. The group of timing diagrams is used to describe a specific functionality of the protocol. For example, we extracted timing diagrams for 3 functionality groups from the AMBA AXI Protocol Specification [1]: the master/slave channel handshake process, the reset operation, and the low-power request/acknowledge handshake mechanism. The timing diagrams of the master/slave channel handshake process are shown in Fig. 3.

For each functionality group, the user indicates the relevant signals. The user is also required to extract textual descriptions that explain the target functionality from the documents. This can be a set of rules, a whole section, or even include signal descriptions.

Property Generation. Given relevant signal information, our property generation algorithm generates candidate properties based on a predefined set of templates. An example of such templates is shown in Fig. 4. The properties are generated by replacing the variables in the template with actual signals.

Template If [signal] is [level] and [signal] is [level], then [signal/word] remains stable in the next cycle. Candidate property 1 If VALID is HIGH and READY is LOW, then DATA remains stable in the next cycle. Candidate property 2 If VALID is LOW and READY is HIGH, then DATA remains stable in the next cycle. Candidate property 3 If VALID is LOW and READY is HIGH, then READY remains stable in the next cycle.

*Fig. 4: Example of a template and some of its candidate properties generated by the property generation algorithm.*

SAT-based Property Check. The next step of our framework is to formally check whether the candidate properties hold on the timing diagrams. In this step, each temporal property, along with each timing diagram, will be translated into formulas in propositional logic and checked by Satisfiability (SAT) solvers. The details of how the check is modeled as a SAT problem are described in Section IV-A.

LLM-assisted Property Filtering. Even if a property holds on all timing diagrams, it may still be incorrect with respect to the protocol. For example, candidate property 3 in Fig. 4 would pass the formal property check since it does not violate any timing diagrams in Fig. 3, but it may not be a necessary constraint for a typical master/slave handshake mechanism. Therefore, after the SAT-based property check, an LLM is consulted to check whether the remaining properties are relevant and should hold with respect to the textual descriptions. The LLM serves as a proxy for human engineers, reading the documents and filtering out incorrect properties from an existing set.

Template Set Generation. Finally, the effectiveness of our algorithm depends on the quality of the predefined template set. We develop a grammar-based approach to generate compact yet comprehensive template sets, and explore how the grammar can be refined by studying results of generated formal specifications. The details are discussed in Section III.

Note that both the templates and properties are in abstract syntax tree (AST) format for the Property Generation and SAT-based Property Check tools to process. Our tool also translates them into formats such as natural language (as shown in Fig. 4) and SVA. The LLM reads the natural language format, and the SVA format can be used by formal verification tools for various applications.

## III Template and Property Set Generation

As a template-based framework, Flag cannot generate a property if its structure is not included in the template set. On the other hand, if the template set is too large, the tool can end up generating millions of candidate properties, creating a burden on the checking algorithms. Therefore, a systematic approach is required to develop succinct yet comprehensive template sets.

### III-A Experience-based Template Set Development

At first glance, it may seem that an extremely large template set is required to cover all the SVA properties needed for various protocols. However, since communication protocols primarily regulate data transfer mechanisms, we find that a fairly simple set of structures is usually sufficient to cover most properties. For example, among all our experiments we have not seen a case requiring complex SVA operators such as non-consecutive repetition ([=m:n]). It is also unlikely that a complex chain of various operators such as $rose(sig1) && $fell(sig2) && sig3 == val would be needed.

Moreover, we observe that SVA properties required for various protocols share similar structures. For example, the template shown in Fig. 4 is a typical structure for master/slave handshake mechanisms. This handshake mechanism appears in various communication protocols, including AXI, WISHBONE and PCI. Therefore, by studying property structures on previously solved cases, we can construct templates that are useful for other protocols.

Based on these observations, we propose an iterative approach to develop succinct yet comprehensive template sets. As Fig. 2 illustrates, the template set can be refined based on inspections of previous results to improve our framework in the future.

### III-B Grammar-based Template Set Generation

It can be challenging to maintain a template set as it gradually gets refined. For example, when adding a new template, the user would have to read the entire set to check whether it is redundant. If the set gets too large, it is also difficult to determine which templates to delete or modify. To solve these issues, we allow users to define grammars that are more succinct and readable, compared to unstructured template sets.

A grammar consists of terminal symbols, non-terminal symbols, and a set of production rules (one for each non-terminal). In our framework, the terminals include (1) fixed SVA operators and (2) variables, including signal (<signal>, <word>) and value (<level>, <value>) types. The grammar can generate many sentences over the terminal symbols by making some choice in each production rule, beginning with the top-level production rule.

In the example grammar shown in Fig. 5, the top-level rule defines an implication non-terminal, denoted $\langle$ implic $\rangle$ , which comprises an SVA implication operator (|->), a conjunction ( $\langle$ conj $\rangle$ ) non-terminal and a delay ( $\langle$ delay $\rangle$ ) non-terminal. Note that the conjunction rule has two choices in the grammar – it can conjoin (&&) two or three assignments ( $\langle$ assign $\rangle$ ). Similarly, the delay rule has two choices – it delays by one cycle (##1) either an assignment or a stable non-terminal. The assignment rule equates (==) a signal and its level, and the stable rule comprises the stable operator ($stable) on either a signal or a word.

In our grammars, each sentence generated by the top-level rule corresponds to a template. Note that each template has fixed SVA operators and the variables for signal and value types, where the variables will be filled in later during property generation. In particular, the template shown in Fig. 4 can be generated by the grammar in Fig. 5.

$$ \displaystyle\langle\textrm{implic}\rangle \displaystyle::= \displaystyle\textbf{{|->}}\;\langle\textrm{conj}\rangle\;\langle\textrm{delay}\rangle \displaystyle\langle\textrm{conj}\rangle \displaystyle::= \displaystyle\textbf{{\&\&}}\;\langle\textrm{assign}\rangle\;\langle\textrm{assign}\rangle\;\mid\; \displaystyle\textbf{{\&\&}}\;\langle\textrm{assign}\rangle\;\langle\textrm{assign}\rangle\;\langle\textrm{assign}\rangle \displaystyle\langle\textrm{delay}\rangle \displaystyle::= \displaystyle\textbf{{\#\#1}}\;\langle\textrm{assign}\rangle\;\mid\;\textbf{{\#\#1}}\;\langle\textrm{stable}\rangle \displaystyle\langle\textrm{assign}\rangle \displaystyle::= \displaystyle\langle\textrm{stable}\rangle \displaystyle::= $$

*Fig. 5: Example of a simple grammar, where the top-level rule is $\langle$ implic $\rangle$ , and the terminals are (1) SVA operators and (2) signal (<signal>, <word>) and value (<level>) types.*

As shown in Fig. 2, the grammars, as well as template sets, can be refined with the iterative approach by inspecting properties generated for previous protocols. Once a grammar is constructed, our tool automatically generates its corresponding template set.

In Section V-A, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this iterative refinement approach by constructing a single grammar for various communication protocols. However, note that it is also possible to derive specific grammars for targeted scenarios (e.g., deriving a specific grammar for the master/slave handshake mechanism).

### III-C Template-based Property Generation

Given a predefined template set, a straightforward algorithm is implemented to generate the corresponding candidate properties. The users are required to provide the signals and their corresponding types. Using Fig. 4 as an example, VALID is a signal (one-bit signal) and DATA is a word (multi-bit signals). The property generation algorithm simply replaces each variable with actual signals according to its type. Note that in all our experiments, we only specify two signal types – signal and word. However, it is possible to create more types to avoid generating incorrect properties (e.g. creating a reset type for reset signals).

## IV Formal and LLM-based Property Filtering

Given a comprehensive set of candidate properties, the next step is to filter out the incorrect ones with respect to the protocol specification documents. First, a formal approach is used to check and remove properties that are inconsistent with the timing diagrams in the documents. We express both the properties and the timing diagrams as constraints in propositional logic, and then invoke a SAT solver to check their consistency. Next, LLM-based techniques are used to further remove incorrect properties with respect to a textual description extracted from the documents. This section describes the details of the filtering algorithms.

### IV-A SAT-based Property Check

#### IV-A1 Encoding Timing Diagram Constraints

Timing diagrams are used in specification documents to describe specific signal behaviors of the protocol. Such timing diagrams typically consist of signals with explicit, unconstrained, and symbolic values. For example, the timing diagram in Fig. 3(a) can be expressed as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\texttt{DATA }=[\texttt{X, X, V1, V1, X}] \displaystyle\texttt{VALID}=[\texttt{0, 0, 1, 1, 0}] \displaystyle\texttt{READY}=[\texttt{0, 0, 1, 1, 0}] $$

The signal vectors above can also be expressed as constraints on signal values at each clock cycle. As an example, the following constraint can be extracted from the above signal vectors:

$$ \begin{split}\varphi_{td}\leftarrow&(\texttt{DATA[2]}=\texttt{DATA[3]})\wedge\\
&(\texttt{VALID[0]}=\texttt{0})\wedge(\texttt{VALID[1]}=\texttt{0})\wedge...\end{split} $$

This formula defines a set of finite execution traces, which is implied by the timing diagram. Given the signal vector format, our tool automatically generates the constraints in propositional logic.

Note that timing diagrams in protocol specification documents are usually depicted in figure formats. They should be translated to the signal vector format for our tool to process. So far, we find it easy to perform this translation manually, since these descriptive timing diagrams typically contain only a few signals with fewer than 10 clock cycles. In addition, if some text format of these timing diagrams is provided (such as source codes to generate the figure format), it is possible to automatically translate it to the signal vector format.

We have also tried converting the timing diagrams from figure formats to signal vectors using LLMs. However, today’s LLMs are still poor at analyzing the subtleties in figures. For example, LLMs often make mistakes when asked questions such as “What is VALID’s value in each clock cycle?” for the timing diagrams in Fig. 3.

#### IV-A2 Encoding Property Constraints

A temporal property enforces constraints to regulate signal behaviors on a target timing diagram, in addition to the constraints derived from the timing diagram itself.

For example, the following constraint can be derived from candidate property 1 in Fig. 4:

$$ \begin{split}\varphi_{p}\leftarrow&(\texttt{VALID[0]}\wedge\neg\texttt{READY[0]}\rightarrow\texttt{DATA[1]}=\texttt{DATA[0]})\\
&\wedge(\texttt{VALID[1]}\wedge\neg\texttt{READY[1]}\rightarrow\texttt{DATA[2]}=\texttt{DATA[1]})\\
&\wedge...\end{split} $$

It can be seen that the temporal property is “localized” to regulate signal behavior at each clock cycle in the timing diagram.

Algorithm 1 provides a high-level view of our algorithm for encoding property constraints. The algorithm repeatedly calls a procedure localize to enforce the constraints of a candidate property on each clock cycle, and computes the conjunction of the returned propositional formulas.

*Algorithm 1 Encoding property constraints*

```
1: Property (AST format) $prop$
2: Constraint (propositional logic) $\varphi_{p}$
3: $\varphi_{p}\leftarrow True$
4: for $cyc\leftarrow 0$ to $CYC\_MAX$ do
5: $\varphi_{local}\leftarrow$ localize( $prop,cyc$ )
6: if $\varphi_{local}\neq None$ then
7: $\varphi_{p}\leftarrow\varphi_{p}\wedge\varphi_{local}$
8: end if
9: end for
```

Since the property is provided in AST format, the localize function can recursively handle each operator, starting from the top-level operator, to generate the propositional constraint. For some examples, we show how the localize function handles the SVA operators of candidate property 1 in Fig. 4:

- • Equality (==): The equality operator has two operands, signal and value. The localize function returns $\texttt{signal}[cyc]=\texttt{value}$ for this operator.

- • Stable ($stable): This operator has a single signal operand. The formula $\texttt{signal}[cyc]=\texttt{signal}[cyc-1]$ would be returned. The None object (in Python) would be returned if $cyc=0$ .

- • Logical And (&&): This operator has two operands, lhs and rhs. The formula $\textsc{localize}(\texttt{lhs},cyc)\wedge\textsc{localize}(\texttt{rhs},cyc)$ would be returned. However, the None object would be returned if either of the recursive calls returns None.

- • Delay (##1): The formula $\textsc{localize}(\texttt{operand},cyc+1)$ is returned unless $cyc=CYC\_MAX$ , where None would be returned.

- • Implication (|->): This operator has two operands, ante and cons. $\textsc{localize}(\texttt{ante},cyc)\rightarrow\textsc{localize}(\texttt{cons},cyc)$ is returned unless either of the recursive calls returns None, where None would be returned.

Note that equation (2) can be derived by applying Algorithm 1 to candidate property 1 in Fig. 4.

#### IV-A3 Checking Algorithm

Finally, the overview of the SAT-based Property Check step is shown in Algorithm 2. The Encode_td and Encode_prop functions extract the constraints enforced by each timing diagram and candidate property, respectively. Note that a property holds on a timing diagram if and only if it is impossible to find a valid execution trace on the timing diagram that violates the property. That is, $\varphi_{td}\wedge\neg\varphi_{p}$ is unsatisfiable. Therefore, a SAT solver can be used to check whether each candidate property is valid on the timing diagrams, retaining only the consistent ones.

*Algorithm 2 SAT-based Property Check*

```
1: Timing diagrams $TD$ , candidate properties $CP$
2: Verified properties $VP$
3: for all $td\in TD$ do
4: $VP\leftarrow\phi$
5: $\varphi_{td}\leftarrow\text{Encode\_td($td$)}$
6: for all $prop\in CP$ do
7: $\varphi_{p}\leftarrow\text{Encode\_prop($prop$)}$
8: if sat_solve( $\varphi_{td}\wedge\neg\varphi_{p}$ ) $=unsat$ then
9: $VP\leftarrow VP\cup\{prop\}$
10: end if
11: end for
12: $CP\leftarrow VP$
13: end for
```

#### IV-A4 Optimizations

Aside from the standard check flow, we perform further optimizations on the candidate properties. First, we remove all tautologies (e.g., “If VALID is HIGH, then VALID is HIGH.”) from the candidate set, since they do not add any constraint on signal behaviors. This can be done by checking the property with an entirely unconstrained timing diagram that contains only “X” values. We perform a pre-process step to remove all tautologies before checking them with any provided timing diagrams.

In addition, we do not include vacuous properties in our check. That is, if the antecedent of an implication property never holds on any provided timing diagrams, we automatically remove it from the candidate set since its consequent can never be checked.

### IV-B LLM-based Property Filtering

Given the formally checked property set, we further remove incorrect properties with respect to the textual description of the document. In this step, we provide the formally checked properties (in natural language) and textual description to an LLM, and prompt the model to extract the properties from the given checked set that best describe the details of the textual description. We use the LLM in a zero-shot setting – without any task-specific fine-tuning or in-context examples – relying solely on its pre-trained capabilities.

Due to the inherent stochasticity of LLMs, identical prompts may yield different outputs across multiple runs. To improve the robustness and reproducibility of our results, we issue the same prompt three times and take the union of the resulting sets of rules.

### V-B SAT-based Property Check

Given the candidate properties generated from the complete grammar in Section V-A, we implement the SAT-based property check to remove properties inconsistent with the timing diagrams.

### V-C LLM-assisted Property Filtering

Given the formally checked property set and a textual description from the document, an LLM is then prompted to extract the properties from the formally checked set that best describe the details of the textual description.

Table IV reports the results. The number of formally checked properties is shown in column 3, and the number of LLM-extracted properties is shown in column 4. To analyze the quality of the extracted property sets, we perform a manual inspection and divide the extracted properties into several categories. The results are reported in the remaining columns:

- • covered: We analyze whether each target property is covered by the extracted property set. The target properties are further divided into explicit and inferred sets, where the explicit properties are obtained by analyzing the textual descriptions, while the inferred properties are not explicitly described in the textual descriptions but derived based on the user’s understanding of communication protocols. Note that there are multiple ways to describe a temporal constraint with SVA properties. For example, the semantics of a target property may be covered by two distinct properties from the LLM-extracted set. Therefore, when analyzing whether a target property is covered, we consider the full extracted set.

- • correct: This category consists of the properties that are correct with respect to the protocol specifications. It can be further divided into unique and redundant sets. A property is unique if it enforces constraints on signal behavior that are not covered by any other properties. A property is redundant if removing it would not affect the semantics of the remaining unique set.

- • incorrect: A property is categorized as incorrect if it violates the textual description of the specification document. For example, for the WISHBONE data transfer case, the LLM extracted a property stating that “the acknowledgment signal can be asserted only when the request signal is asserted.” However, the textual description allows the acknowledgment signal to be asserted at any time. Note that these incorrect properties are retained in the formally checked set when the timing diagrams capture only certain conditions, but not all conditions, that are allowed.

- • unsure: Like a human engineer, the LLM may also infer properties that are not indicated in the textual descriptions. Some of them may require further clarification from the user. For example, the LLM inferred from the AXI low-power handshake mechanism that “the acknowledgment signal should be asserted eventually in response to the request signal,” which might hold true but is not mentioned in the specification document. We label these as unsure properties.

- • hallucinated: Finally, the LLM can also hallucinate, where it makes up properties that are not provided in the checked set, even though it is instructed to extract only properties from that set. These properties can be automatically removed from the extracted set.

#### V-C1 Discussion

Compared to other protocols, we obtained much worse results for the PCI Local Bus specification, including the bus transactions (“transactions”) and transaction termination (“termination”) mechanisms. In the following, we discuss some reasons that affect the performance of our framework.

Lack of textual descriptions. To begin with, the PCI transactions case has the most complex data transfer mechanisms among all data transfer protocols in our experiments. We had to add two auxiliary signals to be able to write down the properties required for its functionality. (Note that it is common to use auxiliary signals when deriving complex temporal properties [11].) Apparently, none of these rules are directly indicated in the textual descriptions. We observed that the LLM still tries to infer some rules despite there being a lack of any described in the text. However, in this case, the inferred rules mostly regulate the behavior of auxiliary signals. Even though they are correct, none of them covers the target properties. In conclusion, experienced engineers are still more capable than LLMs in inferring properties when there is a lack of textual description, especially for complex cases.

Limited reasoning capability of LLMs. Even when a target property is explicitly described by the textual description, we have found that LLMs sometimes fail to reason about it. For example, the textual description of the PCI termination case contains the following information:

Note: A # symbol at the end of a signal name indicates that the asserted state occurs when the signal is at low voltage. When the # symbol is absent, the signal is asserted at a high voltage. ... Once a master has asserted IRDY#, it cannot change IRDY# or FRAME# until the current data phase completes. ... A data phase completes on any rising clock edge on which IRDY# is asserted and either STOP# or TRDY# is asserted. From these descriptions, a human engineer can explicitly derive the following rules:

- • If IRDY# is LOW and STOP# is HIGH and TRDY# is HIGH, then IRDY# remains stable in the next cycle.

- • If IRDY# is LOW and STOP# is HIGH and TRDY# is HIGH, then FRAME# remains stable in the next cycle.

However, the o1 reasoning model did not extract these two properties even though they were in the formally checked set. We conduct additional experiments to analyze factors that affect the model’s reasoning capability.

### V-D Comparison of Flag with Previous Work

Previous research has proposed ML-based approaches to generate SVA properties from IC design specification documents for RTL design and verification purposes [12, 13, 14]. We demonstrate the limitations of such approaches in generating formal specifications for on-chip communication protocols.

The AssertLLM framework [14] incorporates three customized LLMs that deal with decomposed tasks to generate SVAs from specification documents. Two of the LLMs are used to extract information from (1) textual descriptions, and (2) waveforms (timing diagrams) in the specification documents. The third LLM is used to translate the extracted information into SVAs. The generated SVAs are categorized into three types: bit-width, connectivity, and function. Since the first and second types are not relevant to signal interactions, we only include the function type SVAs in our results.

Flag solves all these issues by generating necessary properties from a predefined grammar and automatically translating them into SVA. A formal approach is used to filter out properties inconsistent with timing diagrams, and the LLM is only responsible for extracting properties from the remaining set.

## VI Limitations

Timing diagrams. Flag utilizes the unambiguous timing diagrams from the document in its property filtering stage to reduce incorrect properties. For simple protocols such as Q-Channel and P-Channel, all properties required to form the formal specification are described by timing diagrams. However, for more complex protocols, some mechanisms that regulate signal behaviors are merely described in text, possibly complemented with other contexts, such as tables and flowcharts. In our experiments, we focus on the functionality groups that utilize descriptive timing diagrams. Therefore, for more complex protocols (AXI, WISHBONE, APB and PCI), the target properties in our experiments do not cover the entire formal specification.

One alternative is to skip the SAT-based property check and directly extract the necessary properties using LLM-based techniques. However, the performance of the LLM can be hindered if the candidate property set becomes too large (as shown in Section V-C). Another solution is to let users create their own timing diagrams. This can be beneficial when the user is not familiar with SVA but understands how the protocol works.

Textual descriptions. The LLM-based property filtering matches the formally checked property set with the textual description to retain only necessary properties. However, as discussed in Section V, some properties are not described by text and are inferred based on the user’s general understanding of communication protocols. In Section V-C, we have observed that LLMs do have some capability in inferring properties, but are not as good as an experienced engineer. It is also shown that text quality affects LLMs’ reasoning ability.

In our experiments, we tried not to modify the way the texts were written when extracting them from the documents. However, note that users can provide their own textual descriptions, possibly by modifying the original documents and adding more information.

In summary, Flag aims to assist, but not replace, its users in deriving formal specifications for on-chip communication protocols.

## VII Related Work

Sentence-level NL to SVA translation. Numerous studies have worked on translating natural language sentences to SVA properties. These sentences are provided in a format that directly describes temporal behaviors of several signals, possibly obtained by analyzing design or protocol specification documents. Natural language processing (NLP) techniques are then used to translate these sentences into SVA. This includes more traditional grammar- and rule-based methods [22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30] and emerging ML technologies such as LLMs [15, 12, 16, 31, 32, 33, 34, 14, 35].

Information extraction from specification documents. In addition to sentence-level SVA translation, several works have addressed the problem of extracting property-related information from specification documents. SpecToSVA [12] developed an ML classifier to identify sentences that correspond to functional properties from IC design specifications, before translating them into SVA. ChIRRAG [13] manually modifies design specifications into a specific format with distinctive labels, and prompts an LLM to generate SVA properties directly from the modified specifications. The generated assertions are further verified in a simulation environment, and the prompt will be manually and repeatedly refined based on the errors. AssertLLM [14] incorporates multiple LLMs to deal with decomposed tasks, including extracting structured information from documents and translating them into SVAs.

These approaches primarily focus on generating SVA properties for RTL debugging. Our evaluation of AssertLLM in Section V-D demonstrated that LLMs are poor at precisely extracting the required information from protocol specification documents. Furthermore, LLMs can generate problematic SVAs, even including syntax errors. Flag solves these issues by combining formal approaches with LLM-based techniques.

Generating assertions from other sources. Previous works have also considered other sources from which SVA or other forms of temporal assertion can be generated. For example, numerous works have considered generating temporal assertions from hardware simulation traces with static analysis and data mining approaches [36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 43]. Other approaches study the structures of SVA properties for specific applications to construct specifications or “property libraries.” Given an RTL design of the application, SVAs can then be automatically generated based on these predefined specifications [44, 45]. More recently, researchers have also considered the use of LLMs to generate SVAs directly from RTL source codes [46, 47]. These works are orthogonal to ours and could be used in combination with the Flag framework.

## VIII Conclusions and Future Work

We propose Flag, a two-stage framework that combines formal and LLM-based techniques to help hardware engineers construct formal protocol specifications from informal documents. We evaluated the effectiveness of Flag for generating SVA properties from specification documents of various open-source on-chip communication protocols, and demonstrated that it outperforms a state-of-the-art SVA generation framework. In addition, we analyze cases where Flag missed many target properties and identify factors that affect its performance.

Future work will focus on improving the algorithms to handle these challenging cases, following the directions pointed out in Section V-C. In general, it is also worth exploring more advanced LLM technologies, such as few-shot learning and fine-tuning.

Introduction There is great interest in the fundamental chemistry of hydrocarbon partial oxidation via C–H bond activation using dioxygen as the terminal oxidant. However, despite extensive research, the selective partial oxidation of alkanes stands among the most challenging chemical reactions.1 The high bond dissociation energy of alkane C–H bonds (typically > 96 kcal/mol) combined with the often weaker C–H bonds of functionalized products frequently leads to cascading oxidation reactions and undesirable overoxidation, including the production of carbon dioxide.2 As a result, current industrial processes for the production of methanol from methane rely on an indirect route involving the conversion of methane to synthesis gas (i.e., syngas, CO/H2), which is energy and capital intensive.3 Hence, there is motivation for new processes for the direct partial oxidation of alkanes under ambient conditions.4 While examples of thermal alkane partial oxidation using transition metals have been reported, many of them either have not been tested for light alkanes,5 yield over-oxidized products,6 require complex catalysts and/or multi-step and energy-intense extraction procedures,6a, 7 or make use of terminal oxidants not recycled by dioxygen, preventing industrial viability.8

The Catalytica process, which uses a Pt(II) catalyst in oleum, stands out as it provides high selectivity and conversion of methane to methylbisulfate, which can be hydrolyzed to form methanol.9 Catalytic conversion of methane to methylbisulfate has been demonstrated for other electrophilic catalysts [i.e., in addition to Pt(II)] in superacidic media.10 However, drawbacks of such processes include the susceptibility of the electrophilic metal center to poisoning by even strong acids and the energy intensive process required to separate methyl bisulfate from oleum.

Recently, there has been growing interest in photo-driven C–H functionalization with some advancements on strategies for C–C coupling.11 Photochemistry can allow the selective formation of high-energy intermediates that cannot be obtained thermally. However, there is little precedent regarding photolytic conversion of light alkanes, and only a few publications report the oxidation of non-functionalized alkanes using photocatalysis. Turnovers are attained for conversion of light alkanes to tert-butoxycarbonyl-protected hydrazines using cerium chloride photocatalysts.12 Selective conversion of methane to methanol using a TiO2 supported Fe catalyst and H2O2 as a terminal oxidant was reported,13 as well as aqueous photo-oxidation of methane to methanol with perrhenate salts.14 Previously, our groups have reported oxy-esterification of light alkanes in trifluoroacetic acid (HTFA), in both thermal and photolytic processes,15a-d and the groups of Goldberg and Schelter have reported an aerobic photocatalytic process for alkane iodination.15e

## Results and discussion

We screened a series of commercial, air-stable FeIII compounds for alkane photo-oxidation. For these initial screens, we used reactions that are stoichiometric in FeIII. Iron 1,3,5- benzenetricarboxylate (Fe-BTC) and [Et4N]FeCl4 previously have been shown to functionalize C– H bonds of cyclohexane and toluene in organic solvents under photochemical conditions in the presence of an external oxidant (air/O2).16 For our initial screening, FeIII compounds (0.25 mmol) were combined with HTFA and cyclohexane (1.25 mmol), and the mixture was irradiated with a 370 nm LED for 24 h (Table 1). Of the Fe compounds we examined, commercial FeIII trifluoromethanesulfonate (Fe(OTf)3) performed the best, giving a quantitative yield of cyclohexyl-trifluoroacetate (Cy-TFA), based on amount of FeIII, with no detectable overoxidation (e.g., cyclohexanone or difunctionalized products). The quantitative yield based on FeIII is the theoretical maximum for a two-electron reaction, assuming that two FeIII centers are required for conversion of cyclohexane and HTFA to Cy-TFA (note: these initial screening reactions were

We studied the effect of dioxygen and water on methane oxidation using freshly prepared anhydrous Fe(TFA)3 handled in an anaerobic environment (Table 3). While dioxygen was required to oxidize methane to MeTFA using Fe(TFA)3, the presence of water was detrimental to activity. A key challenge for the selective partial oxidation of light alkanes is over oxidation, which is often a result of the intrinsically high reactivity of functionalized alkyl products compared with starting alkanes. To determine the potential efficacy of Fe-catalyzed photo-driven hydrocarbon partial oxidation, we compared the rate of MeTFA formation from methane to the rate of MeTFA consumption under reaction conditions. The degradation rate of MeTFA under reaction conditions was assessed and shown to be much slower than the rate of its formation, with > 90% MeTFA remaining after 24 h (Figure 3). Regardless of the mechanism for the formation of MeTFA, the mono oxidized product is stable under reaction conditions, indicating a protective effect of the ester moiety.15 Under the conditions in Figure 3, the different solubilities of methane and MeTFA play a role. While methane oxidation proceeds under ideal conditions (before substrate depletion or catalyst decomposition), the rate of MeTFA formation is ~ 16 times faster than the rate of MeTFA degradation. Hence, any significant CO2 production does not likely originate from overoxidation of MeTFA, demonstrating the viability of high selectivity at high conversion of methane.

A pressurized J-Young NMR tube was used to observe gaseous, proton-containing by-products. Upon photolysis of Fe(TFA)3 in HTFA with 50 psig of methane, we detected difluoromethyl trifluoroacetate (CHF2CO2CF3, δ = 6.91 ppm, triplet, 2JHF = 70 Hz) and trace trifluoromethane (CHF3, δ = 6.18 ppm, quartet, 2JHF = 80 Hz),20 both of which are known HTFA degradation products (Figure 4).21 Replacing the methane with Ar, both CHF2CO2CF3 and CHF3 were observed, but formation of MeTFA was not detected (Figure 4). Furthermore, upon replacing HTFA with deuterated trifluoroacetic acid (DTFA), only trace CHF2CO2CF3 and CHF3 were observed under either Ar or CH4 atmosphere. Under these conditions, the formation of small amounts of CHF2CO2CF3 and CHF3 likely arise from trace protio-HTFA remaining in DTFA. These observations point to HTFA degradation, and not that of methane, as the origin of these by-products. This was also observed for the oxidation of substrates with weaker C–H bonds than that of methane, such as propane (Figure S4) and cyclohexane (Figure S12) in DTFA/TFAA. However, CHF3 formation during the oxidation of cyclohexane was observed even in DTFA/TFAA, pointing to the more reactive nature of the cyclohexane C–H bond compared to that of lighter alkanes, and the consequent ability of a CF3 radical to abstract this hydrogen atom.

Summary and Conclusions We report here new reactivity for several commercial FeIII salts for the photo-oxidation of a variety of linear and cyclic alkanes, C1 to C6. From our initial observations, we concluded that a range of FeIII sources soluble in HTFA converged toward a common pathway, leading us to investigate a likely formed complex, Fe(TFA)3, as the active species. We found this complex active for the oxidation of methane, and we characterized a poisoned state of the catalyst that arose from reaction of the active species with water. As water is an expected by-product of alkane oxidation, we developed conditions that remove the water as the reaction proceeded and observed catalytic turnover for the oxidation of methane to MeTFA. Notably dioxygen was determined to be the terminal oxidant, and 17% conversion of methane to the mono-ester product was attained at more than 50% selectivity.
